title: TA9-17094
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (principal claimant), XXXX XXXX (wife), and XXXX XXXX (minor child), claim refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

The specifics of the claims are stated in the narrative to the principal claimant's Personal Information Form (PIF).1 The following is a summary: * The claimants are ethnic Albanians and citizens of Macedonia. * In 2005, a horse owned by the claimants' neighbor, XXXX XXXX, wandered into the claimants' yard. The principal claimant's son chased the horse and got kicked in the head. * The principal claimant's father (XXXXX) shot the horse. An argument ensued between him and XXXX XXXX. As a result, XXXXX shot and wounded XXXX. * A blood feud was declared in 2005 by the XXXX family against the claimants' family. * The principal claimant approached the elders of the village to reconcile his family with the XXXX family with no success. * In XXXX 2008, the principal claimant's elder son was attacked by a member of the XXXX family. * In XXXX 2008, the principal claimant was also attacked by members of the XXXX family but was able to escape injuries. * Fearing for their lives, the claimants fled Macedonia, arrived in Canada on XXXX, 2009, and filed their refugee protection claim on July 28, 2009.

I find that the claimants are not Convention refugees under section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. I also find that, on a balance of probabilities, the claimants are not persons in need of protection under section 97 (1)(b) of the IRPA. ANALYSIS Identity
I find that the claimants are citizens of Macedonia. This has been established by prima facie evidence of their Macedonian passports.2 Nexus

The claimants' fear of the XXXX family arising from a blood feud does not establish a nexus to the Convention refugee definition. This finding is supported by a number of Federal Court decisions, which ruled that victims of criminality, including vendettas, cannot generally establish a nexus to the Convention refugee definition. "Revenge killing in a blood feud has nothing to do with the defence of human rights. Families engaged in them do not form a particular social group for Convention purposes. Recognition of a social group on this basis would have the anomalous result of according status to criminal activity."3 Therefore, their claims under section 96 fail. Section (97)(1)(b) Credibility/Well-Foundedness of Fear
The principal claimant did not provide credible evidence to support the central allegations of their claim.

The principal claimant stated in his narrative that a blood feud was declared by the XXXX family against his family in 2005 and that although the elders of the village tried to resolve the situation, the XXXX family insisted that they were "owed blood" by the claimants' family. The panel asked the claimant what he and his family did after the blood feud was declared. Q: What did you do after the blood feud was declared? A: I was forced to protect myself. I self-confined the whole family in the house. Q: Was any member of your family ever attacked by the XXXX family? A: In XXXX, they attacked my elder son. He had an exam in his school. It happened on his way back from school. Q: Who else was attacked in the family? A: I was attacked, as well, in XXXX 2008 on the way home from the XXXX. Q: What were you doing in the XXXX? A: I worked in the XXXX. Q: Did you work every day in the XXXX? A: Whenever I had the opportunity to work there, in a hidden way. Q: How many times did you go to the XXXX from 2005 till 2008? A: All the time.

Upon questioning from counsel, the principal claimant testified that he went to the XXXX between 2005 and 2008 whenever he felt safe to go to the XXXX. When asked how he determined that it was safe to go to the XXXX, he testified that he checked around the house and then did the night shift. The principal claimant also testified that his son attended school with difficulty, did not attend his classes regularly and that his son was attacked when he went to his school to write his exams.

The principal claimant's actions after the blood feud was declared were not consistent with his testimony that he self confined himself and his family for their safety. His venturing outside the protective confines of their house and working in a XXXX from 2005 till 2008 and his son attending his school, although on an irregular basis, undermined the credibility of the risks they faced as a result of the blood feud declared against him and his family. His checking around his house to determine if it was safe for him to go and work in the XXXXand doing the night shift is not only unreasonable but also not credible, and does not lend credence to the well-foundedness of the claimants' fear.

The principal claimant also gave evidence that his maternal uncle approached the elders of the village to try to resolve or negotiate a settlement between their family and the XXXX family. He also testified that the elders of the village are a group of elders and act together as a group. He further testified that blood feuds are prevalent and widespread in his village and it is the same elders who are approached to bring about reconciliation between the parties. The claimants submitted a letter4 from XXXX XXXX, supposedly an elder in the village, stating the efforts taken by his group to reconcile the parties. When asked why the letter was signed by XXXX XXXX only and not by the other elders, and why there was no mention as to why and when the blood feud was declared, the principal claimant simply stated that he did not know. This letter is supposed to be the official statement from the elders regarding the blood feud between the claimants and the XXXX families. Not only was it not signed by the other elders acting as a group, there is also no mention as to when and why the blood feud was declared. Moreover, the letter from XXXX XXXX was written on a plain piece of paper with no semblance whatsoever of being an official statement from the elders of the village. I give very little probative value to this letter. When asked if he knows of other blood feud incidents in Macedonia given his testimony that blood feuds are widespread in Macedonia, the principal claimant stated that he was not aware of other incidents. When asked to explain the apparent inconsistency of his statements, he stated that he could only testify to his own case and if it happened to other persons, he did not know. I find his explanation not reasonable and credible and I draw an adverse credibility inference. While there is a presumption of truth to allegations made by the claimant under oath, when there are reasons to doubt their truthfulness, then that presumption does not apply. Given the principal claimant's actions after the alleged blood feud was declared, which were not consistent with the risks associated with a family against whom a blood feud was declared, and the questionable statement from the elders from the village, I am not convinced of the truthfulness of the blood feud and ultimately, the well-foundedness of the claimants' fear.

The principal claimant's overall testimony does impact negatively on his credibility and, ultimately, on the well-foundedness of the claimants' alleged fear. A lack of credible evidence going to the subjective element of the claim is, in itself, sufficient for the claims to fail. Even without disbelieving every part of a claimant's testimony, a panel may find the claimant so lacking in credibility that it concludes there is no credible evidence relevant to his claim.5 A claimant's contradictory testimony can cast doubt upon the totality of his oral evidence.6 I find that, on a balance of probabilities, the claimants are not Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection under section 97(1)(b), as there is no risk to their lives or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, should they return to Macedonia. There was also no evidence adduced that would support a finding that the claimants face a danger of torture under section 97(1)(a).

Based on the foregoing analysis and considering the totality of the evidence, I find that there is not a reasonable chance or serious possibility of persecution, if the claimants were to return to Macedonia. I also find that, on a balance of probabilities, the claimants would not be personally subjected to a risk of torture, a risk to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, if they were to return to Macedonia. Accordingly, their claims are rejected.
